blocks.text: This guide was put together to help you study for the NCLEX-PN exam, organized the same way the real exam is organized, so your study time goes where the exam actually puts its weight. Go at your own pace. There is no rule that says you must read it in order — use the Contents page to jump straight to whatever topic you want to review that day. Short, regular sessions beat long, rare ones.
Chapters 2 through 9 follow the eight parts of the real 2026 NCLEX-PN blueprint, in the same order the exam weighs them.
Each topic is written as short, plain statements rather than long paragraphs, so a single fact can be reviewed on its own.
Chapter 10 gives you a simple, repeatable method for answering exam-style questions.
Chapter 11 gives you a suggested pace for studying, and where to find more practice.

This is a study aid, not an official NCSBN publication and not a substitute for your nursing program's own materials or a full practice-question bank (see Chapter 11). Always confirm current exam rules and eligibility at ncsbn.org or with your state board of nursing.
The NCLEX-PN (National Council Licensure Examination for Practical Nurses) is the exam used across the U.S. and its territories to license Practical/Vocational Nurses (LPN/LVN).

It is a computer adaptive test: the computer picks each next question based on whether you got the last one right, so the test is different for every person. It stops once it is confident whether you are above or below the passing standard.
Between 85 and 150 questions, up to 5 hours of testing time including breaks.
Passing is based on your ability level compared to a fixed passing standard, not a percentage of questions correct — there is no fixed "70 percent to pass."

topics.title: What kind of role the exam is testing

blocks.text: The LPN/LVN works under the supervision and direction of a registered nurse (RN), physician, or other licensed provider. The exam questions are written with this in mind.
The LPN/LVN collects data (a focused, ongoing check on a patient whose condition is already known) rather than performing the RN's initial, comprehensive assessment of a new or unstable patient.
The LPN/LVN reinforces teaching that an RN has already started, rather than creating and delivering new, initial patient teaching.
The LPN/LVN contributes observations and data to the RN, who is responsible for analyzing that data, forming the nursing diagnosis, and building the plan of care.
The LPN/LVN cares for patients who are stable or whose condition is well-established and predictable; a new, unstable, or rapidly changing patient is generally the RN's assignment.

These distinctions come up constantly on the exam: when a question asks "which patient should the LPN see first" or "who should perform this task," think about whether it fits a stable, already-assessed patient (usually appropriate for the LPN) or a new, unstable, or unpredictable one (usually the RN's role).

The largest single slice of the exam. Covers advocacy, case management, client rights, confidentiality (HIPAA), continuity of care, information technology, informed consent, interdisciplinary teamwork, legal responsibilities, delegation and assignment, and referrals.

topics.title: Assignment and delegation for the LPN

blocks.text: The LPN can be assigned stable patients with predictable, expected outcomes.

The LPN may delegate simple, routine tasks with a predictable outcome to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP/nursing assistants) — for example, taking vital signs on a stable patient, helping with hygiene, or ambulating a stable patient.
The LPN does not delegate the nursing tasks that require professional judgment: care planning, complex assessment, or teaching that has not already been reinforced by another licensed nurse.

When several tasks are listed and you're asked which one the LPN should do first or which patient to see first, prioritize: an unstable or changing patient over a stable one, a new complaint over an existing, known one, and a task within LPN scope over one that needs RN judgment.
Patients have the right to accept or refuse treatment, to be informed about their care, to privacy, and to have their health information protected.

HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) protects patient health information; only share patient information with people directly involved in that patient's care, and only the information they need.

Informed consent is obtained by the provider performing the procedure, not by the nurse; the nurse's role is to witness the patient's signature and to notify the provider if the patient seems confused, hesitant, or has unanswered questions.

An advance directive (living will, healthcare power of attorney) states a patient's wishes for care if they can no longer decide for themselves. A Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) order must be written by a provider, not assumed from an advance directive alone.

SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is a standard, simple structure for reporting a change in a patient's condition to the RN or provider — it keeps a phone call or handoff organized and complete.
If an order seems unclear, incomplete, or unsafe, clarify it with the prescriber before carrying it out. Never guess at an unclear order.

If a nurse makes an error, the priority is first the patient's safety (assess and notify the provider/RN promptly), then completing an incident report as a quality and safety record — the incident report itself is not written into the patient's chart.

title: 3. Safety and Infection Prevention (10-16% of the exam)

blocks.text: Used with every single patient, every time: hand hygiene before and after every patient contact, gloves whenever you might touch blood or body fluid, and a mask/eye protection if splashing is possible.
Hand hygiene remains the single most effective step to prevent the spread of infection.

topics.title: Transmission-based precautions (used in addition to standard precautions)

blocks.text: **Contact precautions** (gown and gloves): for infections spread by touch, such as MRSA, C. difficile, and draining wounds.
**Droplet precautions** (surgical mask when within about 3 feet/1 meter of the patient): for infections spread by coughing or sneezing over short distances, such as influenza and pertussis.
**Airborne precautions** (N95 respirator, special negative-pressure room): for infections that travel on very small particles through the air, such as tuberculosis, measles, and chickenpox.
Check every patient's fall risk (unsteady gait, confusion, certain medications, prior falls).
For a patient at risk: keep the bed in its lowest position, keep the call light within reach, use non-skid footwear, and check on the patient frequently.
Never leave a confused or unsteady patient unattended in the bathroom or standing without support if they are a known fall risk.
A restraint is always a last resort, used only after safer options have been tried, and always requires a time-limited order from a provider.
Once a restraint is in place, check the patient's circulation, skin, and continued need for the restraint regularly (commonly at least every 2 hours), and release/reposition per facility policy.
A restraint is never used for staff convenience or as punishment.
Remember RACE for a fire: Rescue anyone in immediate danger, sound the Alarm, Confine the fire (close doors), Extinguish if small and safe to do or Evacuate.
Remember PASS for using a fire extinguisher: Pull the pin, Aim at the base, Squeeze the handle, Sweep side to side.
Use proper body mechanics when moving or lifting a patient: keep a wide base of support, bend at the knees rather than the back, and keep the patient or load close to your body.

title: 4. Health Promotion and Maintenance (6-12% of the exam)

topics.title: Growth and development across the lifespan

blocks.text: Infants gain a social smile around 6-8 weeks, sit without support around 6-8 months, and often say their first words around 9-12 months.
Toddlers (1-3 years) engage in parallel play (playing near, not with, other children) and often begin toilet-training readiness around 18-24 months.
Preschoolers (3-6 years) engage in more cooperative play and imaginative/magical thinking.
School-age children (6-12 years) place growing importance on friendships and mastering skills.
Adolescents (12-18 years) are forming their sense of identity and are capable of abstract thinking.

Older adults commonly experience gradually slower reflexes, thinner skin (higher skin-injury risk), reduced kidney and liver function (which can change how medications are processed), and some decline in hearing and vision — these are expected aging changes, not automatically signs of illness.

topics.title: Basic antepartum and newborn facts (high yield, kept simple)

blocks.text: A normal pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks from the first day of the last menstrual period.
Warning signs in pregnancy that need prompt reporting to the provider: vaginal bleeding, severe headache with vision changes, a sudden increase in swelling, decreased fetal movement, and fever.
A normal newborn heart rate is about 110-160 beats per minute, and a normal newborn respiratory rate is about 30-60 breaths per minute.

The Apgar score (done at 1 and 5 minutes after birth) checks Appearance (color), Pulse, Grimace (reflex response), Activity (muscle tone), and Respiration; each is scored 0-2, for a total score from 0 to 10.
Encourage regular exercise, a balanced diet, adequate sleep, not smoking, and limited alcohol as basic health-promotion counseling for adults of any age.
Immunizations follow a national schedule that is updated periodically; the LPN reinforces the current recommended schedule rather than needing to memorize every date.
Basic safety counseling for older adults: reduce fall hazards at home (loose rugs, poor lighting), review medications regularly for interactions, and keep regular vision and hearing checks.
Good techniques: open-ended questions, active listening, silence (giving the patient time to think or speak), reflecting the patient's own words back to them, and simply offering your presence.

Things to avoid: asking "why" (it can sound accusatory), giving false reassurance ("everything will be fine"), giving your own unsolicited advice, or changing the subject away from what the patient raised.
When a question asks for "the best response," look for the option that acknowledges the patient's feelings and invites them to say more, rather than the option that gives a quick fix or reassurance.
The commonly taught stages of grief are denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance — people do not always move through them in this order, and that is normal.

Healthy coping looks like talking about feelings, seeking support, and gradually adjusting; concerning signs include withdrawal from all support, ongoing hopelessness, or talk of self-harm, which should always be reported to the RN or provider right away.
If abuse or neglect is suspected, the first priority is the immediate safety of the patient.
Document exactly what you see and exactly what the patient says, using their own words where possible, without asking leading questions.
Nurses are mandated reporters for suspected abuse of children and, in most places, of older or dependent adults — report through the proper channel per your facility and local law.
Depression: persistent low mood or loss of interest, lasting most of the day, most days, for at least two weeks, often with changes in sleep, appetite, and energy.
Anxiety: persistent, excessive worry that interferes with daily life, often with physical symptoms like a racing heart or trouble sleeping.
Any statement suggesting a patient might hurt themselves or someone else should always be taken seriously and reported immediately — never dismissed or kept quiet.

title: 6. Basic Care and Comfort (7-13% of the exam)

blocks.text: Semi-Fowler's (head of bed raised about 30-45 degrees) is a common general position that helps breathing and reduces the risk of aspiration; it's used for most tube feedings.
High Fowler's (head of bed raised 80-90 degrees, nearly sitting up) helps the lungs expand the most and is used for patients having trouble breathing.
Turn and reposition a patient who cannot move themselves at least every 2 hours to protect their skin.

topics.title: Preventing problems from lying still too long (immobility)

blocks.text: Being immobile for a long time can lead to pressure injuries (skin breakdown), blood clots, pneumonia, constipation, and weaker muscles.
Prevention: reposition regularly, help the patient move and walk as soon as it's safe, encourage deep breathing exercises, and make sure they are drinking enough fluids.
Stage 1: the skin is not broken, but there's a red area that does not turn white (blanch) when you press on it.
Stage 2: a shallow open sore or blister, but you cannot see the deeper tissue.
Stage 3: a deeper open wound; you may see fat, but not muscle or bone.
Stage 4: a very deep wound where muscle, tendon, or bone is visible.
Once any pressure injury is found, report it and keep pressure off that area.

For a patient with a swallowing problem (dysphagia): sit them upright for meals, use the thickened-liquid consistency that has been ordered, offer small bites, and watch closely for coughing or choking during meals.
Common special diets: low-sodium (for heart and blood pressure conditions), low-potassium (for some kidney conditions), high-fiber (for constipation), and consistent-carbohydrate (for diabetes).
Keep a urinary catheter bag below the level of the bladder at all times, and keep the tubing free of kinks — this helps urine drain properly and reduces infection risk.
For constipation: encourage fluids, fiber, and walking/movement first, before other measures.
Right patient (check two identifiers, such as name and date of birth), right drug, right dose, right route, right time.
Always check for allergies before giving any medication, and never give a medication if an order is unclear — clarify it first.
Oral (PO), sublingual (under the tongue), intramuscular (IM, into the muscle), subcutaneous (SC/SQ, just under the skin), and intravenous (IV, into the vein) are the main routes you'll be tested on.
Insulin is given by subcutaneous injection, rotating the injection site within the same general area of the body to keep absorption predictable.
A medication meant for one route should never be given by a different route unless specifically ordered.

topics.title: Common medications the LPN should recognize (high level)

blocks.text: **Pain medications (opioids):** watch for slowed breathing and excessive sleepiness; always check the respiratory rate before giving another dose.
**Blood thinners (like warfarin, heparin):** watch for unusual bleeding or bruising; these patients need extra care to prevent injury.
**Diabetes medications (like insulin):** watch for signs of low blood sugar — sweating, shakiness, confusion, hunger — and know that fast-acting sugar treats it right away.

**Heart and blood pressure medications:** check the heart rate and blood pressure before giving many of these, and hold the dose and notify the RN/provider if the readings are outside the safe range you were given.
**Antibiotics:** always check for an allergy first, and complete the full course as ordered even if the patient feels better.

If a patient shows a new, unexpected reaction after a medication (rash, trouble breathing, sudden swelling), stop what you're doing, ensure the patient is safe, and notify the RN or provider immediately.
If you realize a medication error happened, the very first step is to check on the patient's safety, then notify the RN/provider right away, then complete the required incident report.

title: 8. Reduction of Risk Potential (9-15% of the exam)

blocks.text: Part of the LPN's job is noticing when something looks different from a patient's normal pattern — a new complaint, a changed vital sign, new confusion, or a wound that looks different than before — and reporting it promptly to the RN.

A change in level of consciousness (someone becoming more confused, harder to wake, or less responsive) is one of the most important signs to report immediately, since it often signals a serious problem developing.
Normal adult heart rate: about 60-100 beats per minute.
Normal adult respiratory rate: about 12-20 breaths per minute.
Normal adult blood pressure: below about 120/80 mm Hg.
Normal adult temperature: about 36.1-37.2 C (97-99 F); a fever is generally 38.0 C (100.4 F) or higher.
Normal oxygen saturation: 95-100 percent on room air for most people.
After any procedure, the first concerns are always the patient's airway and breathing, then their circulation (watching for bleeding), then their pain and comfort.
Encourage a patient recovering from surgery to turn, cough, and take deep breaths regularly, and to get up and walk as soon as it's considered safe — this helps prevent pneumonia and blood clots.
Watch surgical dressings for excess bleeding or drainage, and report anything unexpected to the RN.

The LPN doesn't need to interpret complex labs independently, but should recognize when a reported result looks clearly abnormal and flag it for the RN. A few commonly referenced normal ranges: blood glucose (fasting) about 70-99 mg/dL, and a normal body temperature range as listed above.
Report any lab value the RN or provider has flagged as needing prompt attention, right away.

Any patient who suddenly looks much worse — struggling to breathe, chest pain, sudden confusion, fainting, or a very abnormal vital sign — needs the RN or provider notified immediately. The LPN's job in this moment is to stay with the patient, keep them safe, and call for help right away — not to try to manage it alone.
Basic life support (CPR) readiness: know your facility's emergency response process and where the emergency equipment is kept, so you can act without delay if needed.

Shock means the body's organs are not getting enough blood flow. Early signs can be subtle: the patient may seem anxious, their skin may feel cool, and their heart rate may be faster than usual, even if blood pressure still looks normal at first.
Later signs are more obvious and dangerous: a real drop in blood pressure, confusion, and reduced urine output. This is always an emergency requiring the RN and provider immediately.

topics.title: Common chronic conditions you'll care for

blocks.text: **Heart failure:** watch for increasing shortness of breath, swelling in the legs, and weight gain over a few days — these suggest fluid is building up and should be reported.

**Diabetes:** watch for signs of both high blood sugar (increased thirst, frequent urination, fatigue) and low blood sugar (shakiness, sweating, confusion) — low blood sugar needs faster action since it can become dangerous quickly.
**COPD/breathing conditions:** watch for increased difficulty breathing, more coughing, or a change in the color or amount of sputum.

After any burn, moving the patient away from the source and cooling the burn area (per facility protocol) are early priorities, along with assessing breathing, especially if the face or airway may have been affected by smoke or heat.

Read the whole question slowly before looking at the answer choices. Ask yourself exactly what it's asking: the very next action, the priority patient, or what shows the patient understood the teaching.

If it's asking "what should you do first," think ABC (Airway, then Breathing, then Circulation) before anything else, and remember that assessing/checking on the patient generally comes before acting, unless the situation is a clear emergency needing immediate action.
If several answers all look reasonable, pick the one that deals with the biggest threat to the patient's safety or life right now.
For "which patient should the LPN see first" questions, an unstable, worsening, or newly changed patient is almost always the answer over a stable, unchanged one.
If an answer choice uses a word like "always" or "never," don't assume it's automatically wrong — check it against what you actually know, the same as any other choice.

topics.title: Staying calm during the real exam

blocks.text: The test stopping "early" does not by itself mean you failed — the computer-adaptive test can end at different points for different people, and that's expected, not a bad sign.
If you don't know an answer, use your best process of elimination rather than leaving it blank, and then move on without dwelling on it — you cannot go back to a previous question on this exam.
A steady pace, regular short breaks in your study routine now, and confidence in what you do know will serve you better than trying to cram everything at once.
Since you are just getting started, there is no need to rush. A steady, repeatable pace works better than trying to do too much at once.
Suggested approach: pick one chapter (2 through 9) per study session. Read it once, then come back the next day and go through the matching section in the practice quiz.
Since Physiological Integrity (the combined weight of Chapters 6-9) makes up the largest overall share of the exam, plan to revisit those four chapters more than once.
Repetition is what makes facts stick — it is completely normal, and expected, to go back over the same chapter more than once.

This guide gives you a foundation and a first set of practice questions, but a real exam-day-ready plan should also include a full practice-question bank with detailed rationales. Well-regarded options include NCSBN's own official practice materials, and established NCLEX-PN review resources such as Kaplan, ATI, Hurst, or Nursing.com. Ask your nursing program which one they recommend, since many programs already have a subscription available to students.

Passing this exam is absolutely something you can prepare for step by step. Go one chapter at a time, be patient with yourself, and celebrate the small wins along the way — every session you complete is real progress.
